newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. may attack Iraq again, doubts surface.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may attack Iraq again, doubts surface.

text.p: The United States said on Sunday it may launch more attacks on Iraq as doubts surfaced again over the wisdom of meting out further punishment to Saddam Hussein.
Asked if more U.S. strikes against Iraq were still possible, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry told a news conference on a brief visit to Kuwait: "Yes, it is still a possibility."

The United States "will take whatever action is necessary" to enforce an expanded southern Iraqi no-fly zone up to the 33rd parallel, which runs 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad, and to protect the pilots who patrol it.

Perry also said he had asked Kuwait's emir, Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah, for permission to proceed with a previously announced plan to deploy 5,000 U.S. troops in the Gulf state. He has also ordered a battery of Scud-busting Patriot missiles to Kuwait to strengthen its air defences.

On a visit to the Gulf to rally the Gulf War alliance against Iraq, Perry dismissed a pledge by Baghdad on Friday to abandon attacks on U.S. planes patrolling the Western-imposed zone, saying: "We cannot rely on Saddam Hussein's promises."

The latest crisis between the United States and Iraq started 15 days ago. Washington punished Iraq for intervening in the faction fighting in its Kurdish north by launching cruise missiles at air defence systems in southern Iraq.

Kuwait, grateful to the United States for leading the 1991 Gulf War that liberated it from a seven-month Iraqi occupation, is so far the only Arab country to support Washington in its latest standoff with Saddam.
But Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Jaber al-Sabah said on Sunday there was no question of U.S. land forces crossing into Iraq from Kuwait.
Russia repeated its criticism of Washington's approach. A Baghdad-based diplomat went as far as saying that Iraq had a right to shoot down planes in the no-fly zones.

"This country has the right to protect itself. When they have warplanes of another country flying over their airspace they have the right to shoot," Vladimir Titorenko, deputy head of the Russian mission in Baghdad, told Reuters in an interview.
He said President Bill Clinton was massing troops in the region so he could win a second term as U.S. president in the election in November.
Iraq stepped up its criticism of the no-fly zones territory and one official newspaper described Clinton as "mentally retarded, immersed in vice and without conscience".
"The imposition of air exclusion zones in the north and south of our country is an aggressive measure by all standards," the ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra said in a front-page editorial.

The government newspaper al-Jumhouriya, which said on Saturday it hoped the decision to suspend missile attacks would ease tension in the Gulf, on Sunday attacked Clinton in some of the strongest language ever used by Iraq against a U.S. leader.
"He is mentally retarded, immersed in vice and without conscience," said a front-page editorial signed by editor-in-chief Salah al-Mukhtar.

The Arab League, which groups all Arabs states including Iraq and Washington's close allies in the Gulf, condemned U.S. cruise missile attacks on Iraq earlier this month, saying they violated Iraqi sovereignty.
While most of its regional allies are unwilling to take part, Washington has pressed on with the buildup in the region, including sending a second aircraft carrier battle group.
The U.S. aircraft carrier Enterprise, with about 75 warplanes aboard, entered the Suez Canal en route to the Gulf.
As the United States pushed ahead with its military buildup in the Gulf, its Kurdish allies in northern Iraq began crossing into Turkey to escape the wrath of Saddam.

About 50 pro-U.S. Kurds, from a group of several hundred brought to the border in a fleet of battered buses, walked across the Habur bridge crossing for passage to Turkey from where they were to be processed for asylum in the United States.
"I feel great. I just want to get across that bridge," said a refugee who identified himself only as Moyyad. A Turkish tank waited on the other side of the border.

As many as 2,500 Iraqi Kurds were to be relocated to a camp in the Turkish town of Silopi. Most worked as employees of U.S. aid programmes and the U.S.-led air operation patrolling a no-fly zone for Iraqi aircraft in northern Iraq. But some are believed to have been engaged in intelligence activities for the Americans.
